title: Gurudongmar Lake from Lachen: Altitude and Safety
meta_description: How the Gurudongmar day works from Lachen, the 4 am start, altitude sickness signs, who should not go, what to carry and the road status since 2023.
summary: Gurudongmar Lake sits at about 5,180 m, reached from Lachen at about 2,750 m by a 3 am start and a 3-hour drive. Stay only 20–40 minutes. Headache and breathlessness are common; children under five, pregnant women and people with heart or lung conditions are advised not to go. Indians only. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The Gurudongmar day, hour by hour
paras: Gurudongmar is not a place you stay; it is a dawn visit from Lachen. On a standard 3-day tour you reach Lachen in the evening of day one, eat early, and sleep a few hours. The driver knocks at about 3 am. You drink tea, collect a packed breakfast, and set off in the dark on a road that climbs past Thangu, at about 3,900 m, and across a high, treeless plateau to the lake. The aim is to arrive soon after sunrise, before the wind rises and clouds build.

You spend 20–40 minutes at the lake, then drive back to Lachen for breakfast, collect your bags, and continue down to Chungthang and up the other valley to Lachung the same afternoon. It is a long day, about 12 hours in the vehicle, and much of it is above 4,000 m.

sections.heading: The lake and its story
paras: Gurudongmar is a glacial lake a few kilometres south of the Tibetan border, with the slopes of Gurudongmar peak behind it. The survey figure for its height is about 5,183 m; the state often quotes 5,430 m. Either way, it is one of the highest lakes in India that a car can reach. From December to May it is mostly frozen; in October its water is a hard, clear blue.

The lake is sacred. The story told in Lachen is that Guru Padmasambhava blessed part of it so that it would not freeze, giving herders water in winter. Some Sikh traditions link it to Guru Nanak. Both are told as lore. Walk quietly, do not throw coins or litter, and do not climb onto the ice.

sections.heading: What altitude does to your body
paras: At 5,180 m each breath carries roughly half the oxygen it does at sea level. You are climbing about 2,400 m in three hours from Lachen, far faster than the 300–500 m a day mountaineers recommend above 3,000 m. Most visitors feel something: a headache, breathlessness on a few steps, a racing heart, nausea, cold hands. That is acute mountain sickness (AMS) in its mild form, and it usually eases quickly once you go down.

The dangerous forms are rare on a short visit but real. Watch for confusion, stumbling, a severe headache that does not ease, vomiting, a wet cough, blue lips, or breathlessness while sitting still. Any of these means go down immediately, give oxygen if you have it, and get medical help at the nearest army or government medical post; your driver knows where it is. Do not wait to see if it passes.
list: Children under five, pregnant women, and people with heart disease, lung disease, uncontrolled blood pressure or severe anaemia are usually advised not to go.
Anyone with a cold, fever or chest infection should skip the lake that day.
Older travellers in good health often manage well; ask your doctor before the trip.
If you are unsure, Lachung and Yumthang give snow and mountains at lower heights.

sections.heading: How to make it safer
paras: Most altitude problems on this trip come from going too high too fast with too little sleep. These steps help.
list: Spend one night in Gangtok before going north, and if you can, two nights in Lachen instead of one.
Drink 2–3 litres of water the day before and warm water on the way up.
Skip alcohol and sleeping pills the night before.
Eat a light dinner early and something small at Thangu.
At the lake, walk slowly, do not run, and keep the stop to 20–40 minutes.
Carry a portable oxygen can, ₹500–900 in Gangtok or Lachen, for emergencies.
Ask your doctor about acetazolamide (Diamox) before the trip; do not start it on a stranger's advice.

sections.heading: What to wear and carry
paras: Before dawn at Gurudongmar the temperature can be −10 to −20 °C in winter and well below freezing even in October and May, with wind. Dress in layers: thermal top and bottom, a fleece, a down or padded jacket, and a windproof outer layer. Rent knee-high boots and a long coat in Lachen for ₹100–300 each if you do not have your own. Add woollen socks, gloves, a cap that covers your ears, sunglasses and sunscreen.

In your day bag: water, dry fruit and chocolate, any regular medicines, a small torch for the 3 am start, toilet paper, and a bag for your rubbish. Phones rarely have signal beyond Lachen, so tell someone your plan.

sections.heading: Permits, access and road status
paras: Gurudongmar is open to Indian nationals only, on a North Sikkim permit arranged by a registered Gangtok tour operator; foreigners are not allowed. The army controls the road above Thangu and can close it at short notice for weather or other reasons.

The bigger issue since October 2023 is the road to Lachen itself. The South Lhonak lake burst and the Teesta flood that followed destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang and long stretches of road, and the Lachen side has been the slowest part of North Sikkim to reopen, with further closures after monsoon landslides. Some seasons Gurudongmar tours have not run at all while Lachung stayed open. Ask two agents what is open that week, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: About 5,180 m by survey figures; the Sikkim government often quotes 5,430 m (17,800 ft). Either way it is far higher than anything most visitors have been to, and you drive up from Lachen, around 2,750 m, in about three hours. Altitude sickness is common, so keep the visit short.

It is risky for young children. Children under five are usually advised not to go, because they cannot tell you clearly how they feel and altitude sickness can develop quickly. Older children in good health often manage a 20–30 minute visit. Watch for listlessness, vomiting or unusual sleepiness, and go down at once if you see them.

faqs.q: How long can you stay at Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: Around 20–40 minutes is what drivers and the army advise. Longer stays raise the risk of altitude sickness. Walk slowly, take your photographs, offer a prayer if you wish, and head back. If anyone in the group feels unwell, leave immediately; symptoms usually ease as you drop toward Thangu and Lachen.

faqs.q: Should I take Diamox for Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Ask your doctor before the trip. Acetazolamide (Diamox) can help prevent acute mountain sickness when started a day before going high, but it has side effects and does not suit everyone, including people with sulfa allergies. Never take it on a stranger's advice, and remember it does not replace going slowly and coming down if unwell.

faqs.q: What time do you leave Lachen for Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: Usually between 3 and 4 am. The aim is to reach the lake soon after sunrise, before wind and cloud build up, and to have time to drive on to Lachung the same day. Your lodge packs tea and breakfast. Sleep early and lay out warm clothes the night before.

No. Gurudongmar is open to Indian nationals only, on a North Sikkim permit arranged by a registered Gangtok tour operator. Foreign nationals with a Protected Area Permit have usually been allowed only as far as Lachung and Yumthang. Check current status before you travel, as rules change.

It depends on the week. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood, the Lachen road and Chungthang crossing have closed for long spells, and snow or army restrictions close the lake road too. Ask two Gangtok agents, read the Mangan district notices, and check current status before you travel and again the evening before you leave.

faqs.q: What are the signs of altitude sickness?
faqs.a: Mild signs are headache, breathlessness, nausea, dizziness and poor sleep. Serious signs are confusion, stumbling, a severe headache that will not ease, repeated vomiting, a wet cough, blue lips, or breathlessness at rest. Serious signs mean go down at once, use oxygen if available, and get medical help at the nearest army or government post.

faqs.q: Do oxygen cans help at Gurudongmar?
faqs.a: They give short relief, which is useful in an emergency on the way down, but they do not prevent altitude sickness and are no substitute for descending. A portable can costs ₹500–900 in Gangtok or Lachen. Carry one per vehicle or per family, and keep it for someone who really needs it.
